title: Αἴλουρος καὶ μύες
part: The Cat and the Mice (Chambry 13 · Perry 79)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 13 (= Perry 79). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », [ ] for words Chambry deletes as interpolated). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἔν τινι οἰκίᾳ πολλοὶ μύες ἦσαν.
sentences.tr: En tini oikiāi polloi myes ēsan.
sentences.l: In a certain house there were many mice.
sentences.n: τις is an enclitic — a word with no accent of its own that leans back on the word before, which is why Ἔν here carries an accent it would not otherwise have. As an adjective it means “a certain, some”.

sentences.t: Αἴλουρος δὲ τοῦτο γνοὺς ἧκεν ἐνταῦθα καὶ συλλαμβάνων ἕνα ἕκαστον κατήσθιεν.
sentences.tr: Ailouros de touto gnous hēken entautha kai syllambanōn hena hekaston katēsthien.
sentences.l: And a cat, having come to know this, arrived there and, seizing them one by one, kept eating them.
sentences.i: A cat found this out, came there, and caught them one at a time and ate them.
sentences.n: γνούς is the aorist participle of γιγνώσκω, “having come to know” — the aorist participle regularly gives what happened first, before the main verb. ἕνα ἕκαστον, “one each”, means one after another; the imperfect κατήσθιεν gives the repetition. ἥκω means “have come, be here”, so its imperfect ἦκεν is “he had arrived”.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ μύες συνεχῶς ἀναλισκόμενοι κατὰ τῶν ὀπῶν ἔδυνον, καὶ ὁ αἴλουρος μηκέτι αὐτῶν ἐφικνεῖσθαι δυνάμενος, δεῖν ἔγνω δι’ ἐπινοίας αὐτοὺς ἐκκαλεῖσθαι.
sentences.tr: Hoi de myes synechōs analiskomenoi kata tōn opōn edynon, kai ho ailouros mēketi autōn ephikneisthai dynamenos, dein egnō di’ epinoias autous ekkaleisthai.
sentences.l: And the mice, being continually used up, sank down into their holes, and the cat, no longer being able to reach them, decided that he must call them out by a stratagem.
sentences.i: As the mice were steadily consumed they took to sinking down into their holes, and the cat, no longer able to get at them, decided he would have to draw them out by a trick.
sentences.n: ἀναλισκόμενοι, “being spent, used up”, is a word for expenditure — a cold way to say what was happening to them. ἐφικνέομαι takes the genitive of what one reaches (αὐτῶν). ἔγνω is the same verb as γνούς just above, here at its other end of meaning: from “perceive” to “resolve”. δεῖν, an impersonal infinitive, carries what he resolved: that it was necessary.

sentences.t: Διόπερ ἀναβὰς ἐπί τινα πάσσαλον καὶ ἑαυτὸν ἐνθένδε ἀποκρεμάσας προσεποιεῖτο τὸν νεκρόν.
sentences.tr: Dioper anabas epi tina passalon kai heauton enthende apokremasas prosepoieito ton nekron.
sentences.l: Therefore, having climbed up onto a peg and having hung himself down from there, he pretended to be the corpse.
sentences.i: So he climbed up onto a peg, hung himself down from it, and played dead.
sentences.n: Two aorist participles and then the imperfect main verb — the participle chain that runs these fables. προσποιέομαι is “pretend, feign”, and τὸν νεκρόν is what he pretends to be: the article makes it the dead thing on the peg, the particular part he is playing. A πάσσαλος is a wooden peg driven into the wall, the ordinary household hook.

sentences.t: Τῶν δὲ μυῶν τις παρακύψας, ὡς ἐθεάσατο αὐτόν, εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’, ὦ οὗτος, σοί γε, κἂν θύλαξ γένῃ, οὐ προσελεύσομαι. »
sentences.tr: Tōn de myōn tis parakypsas, hōs etheasato auton, eipen: « All’, ō houtos, soi ge, kan thylax genēi, ou proseleusomai. »
sentences.l: And one of the mice, having peeped out, when he beheld him, said: « But, you there, to you at any rate, even if you should become a meal-sack, I shall not come near. »
sentences.i: One of the mice put its head out, and when it had looked at him said, « No, my friend — even if you turn into a meal-sack, I am not coming near you. »
sentences.n: ὦ οὗτος is the everyday way of hailing someone, “hey, you there” — colloquial and a shade rude. κἄν is καὶ ἐάν run together (crasis), “even if”, with the subjunctive γένῃ. A θύλαξ is a sack, usually leather, for meal or grain — the sort of thing that hangs from a peg, which is presumably why the mouse reaches for it; the fable does not say so outright.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ φρόνιμοι τῶν ἀνθρώπων, ὅταν τῆς ἐνίων μοχθηρίας πειραθῶσιν, οὐκέτι αὐτῶν ταῖς ὑποκρίσεσιν [οὗτοι] ἐξαπατῶνται.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hoi phronimoi tōn anthrōpōn, hotan tēs eniōn mochthērias peirathōsin, ouketi autōn tais hypokrisesin [houtoi] exapatōntai.
sentences.l: The story shows that the sensible among men, whenever they have made trial of the badness of certain people, are no longer deceived by their play-acting.
sentences.i: The story shows that sensible men, once they have had a taste of certain people's badness, are no longer taken in by their performances.
sentences.n: Square brackets are Chambry's mark for words he judges a later intrusion and would delete: [οὗτοι], “these men”, is printed but not treated as the author's. Angle brackets ⟨ ⟩ mean the opposite — words he supplies. They are kept visible here because the text is a reconstruction and it is better to see the editor at work than to be handed a clean page. ὅταν with the subjunctive (πειραθῶσιν) is the indefinite “whenever”; πειράομαι takes the genitive of what is tried. ὑπόκρισις is the actor's word — playing a part, as the cat did on his peg.
